title: Expression Arrays: Normalization Assumptions, Degraded RNA and the mRNA–Protein Gap
summary: Learn what median scaling and quantile normalization each assume, when those assumptions fail, how DASL profiles degraded FFPE RNA, and why an mRNA change on an array does not prove a protein change.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 70 Hits 12 (median vs quantile normalization) and 15 (DASL for degraded RNA) and Traps 5 (mRNA vs protein) and 6 (quantile assumption). Checked against Hicks 2015, Zhao 2020, Park 2003, April 2009 and Vogel 2010 (all read as Europe PMC full text). The sources describe median correction and trimmed-mean scaling; the reviewer’s “median-intensity normalization” is taught as median scaling. Hit 15’s 1536-target limit applies to the original DASL assay; April 2009 describes a whole-genome DASL covering about 24,000 RefSeq genes, so the lesson gives both (register flag proposed). Not taught: nylon macroarray autofluorescence (Hit 9, Trap 1), for which no readable open source was found.

objectives: State the assumption behind median (or trimmed-mean) scaling and behind quantile normalization.
Recognise when global normalization can remove real biological differences and name two ways to respond.
Explain how DASL profiles degraded FFPE RNA and why array mRNA changes do not prove protein changes.

scenes.title: Brighter arrays, old blocks, a bold claim
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: a research team compares tumour and normal expression arrays. (1) The tumour arrays look brighter overall than the normal arrays. (2) For follow-up they only have archived formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) blocks. (3) A colleague says a gene that rose 3-fold on the array “proves the protein is up”. Question token: “Normalize how, profile what, conclude what?”

cues.text: Invented scenario. A team compares tumour and normal expression arrays, and the tumour arrays look brighter overall.
Their follow-up samples are old formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded blocks, with damaged RNA.
And a colleague says a gene that rose three-fold on the array proves the protein went up. Which normalization, which assay, and which conclusion?

props.label: Normalize how, profile what, conclude what?

scenes.title: What normalization assumes
scenes.altText: Schematic: two arrays drawn as intensity histograms. Card 1: normalization removes technical variation between arrays; global adjustment methods assume that global differences between samples are technical, not biological. Card 2: median or trimmed-mean scaling shifts each array by one factor so a central value matches; the trimmed-mean method assumes most genes are not differentially expressed. Card 3: quantile normalization in four steps (sort each sample, average each rank across samples, replace values with the rank average, restore original order). Card 4: result: every sample ends up with the same distribution; the method assumes the distributions really are the same.

cues.text: Normalization removes technical differences between arrays, such as one array scanning brighter. Global methods all assume that differences across whole samples are technical, not biology.
Median or trimmed-mean scaling moves each array by a single factor so a central value lines up. The assumption is modest: most genes are not differentially expressed.
Quantile normalization goes further. Sort each sample, average each rank across samples, replace every value with its rank average, then put the genes back in order.
Every sample now has an identical intensity distribution, so quantile normalization assumes the whole distribution really is the same across samples.

scenes.title: When the assumption is wrong
scenes.altText: Card: “Many genes change in one group” — if a large share of genes are expected to differ between groups (one study cites cancers as an example of a strong class effect), global normalization can remove real biological variation. Card: distortions reported when normalization assumptions are violated — false positives, shrunken effect sizes and masked true effects (false negatives). Card: options from the sources — test the assumption first (quantro, a permutation test for global distribution differences between groups); if quantile normalization must be used with strong class effects, normalize within each class (“class-specific” strategy).

cues.text: The assumption is fair when only a minority of genes change. But if many genes differ in one group, global normalization can erase real biology. One study names cancer as an obvious example of a strong class effect.
When the assumption is violated, the reported distortions run both ways: false positives, shrunken effect sizes, and true effects masked as false negatives.
So test the assumption first. The quantro method checks whether groups differ in their whole intensity distributions before global normalization is applied.
And if quantile normalization must be used when classes differ strongly, one study recommends normalizing within each class separately, the class-specific strategy.

props.label: Must use quantile? Normalize per class

scenes.title: Degraded RNA, and what an array measures
scenes.altText: Card: FFPE RNA — formalin makes adenosines prone to chemical modification and fragments RNA; up to half the fragments may lack a poly-A tract, a problem for oligo-dT-primed methods. Card: DASL (cDNA-mediated annealing, selection, extension and ligation): random priming during cDNA synthesis, a short ~50-nucleotide target per probe; the original assay profiled up to 1536 targets; the 2009 whole-genome version covered about 24,000 RefSeq genes. Card: mRNA is not protein — in one human cell line mRNA level alone explained under a third of protein-abundance variation; adding sequence features linked to translation and protein degradation explained about two-thirds. Hook answers card.

cues.text: Formalin fixation fragments RNA and chemically modifies adenosines. Up to half of the fragments may have no poly-A tail, so methods that prime only from oligo-dT struggle.

The DASL assay gets around this with random priming and a short target of about fifty nucleotides per probe. The original assay profiled up to 1536 targets; a 2009 whole-genome version covered about twenty-four thousand genes.

An array measures transcripts, not proteins. In one human cell line, mRNA level alone explained under a third of the variation in protein abundance; adding sequence features linked to translation and protein degradation raised that to about two-thirds.

Back to the hook. Test the global-distribution assumption before normalizing brighter tumour arrays, use a degradation-tolerant assay like DASL for FFPE blocks, and confirm protein changes at the protein level.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Quantile normalization only assumes most genes are unchanged” (✓ it forces and assumes identical whole distributions; the most-genes-unchanged assumption belongs to median or trimmed-mean scaling); “An mRNA rise on an array proves a protein rise” (✓ arrays measure transcripts; translation and degradation intervene); “Degraded FFPE RNA cannot be expression-profiled” (✓ DASL uses random priming and short targets designed for degraded RNA).

cues.text: Trap one: quantile normalization only assumes most genes are unchanged. No: it forces identical whole distributions. The most-genes-unchanged assumption belongs to median scaling.
Trap two: an mRNA rise on an array proves a protein rise. No: arrays measure transcripts, and translation and protein degradation intervene.
Trap three: degraded paraffin-block RNA cannot be profiled. No: DASL was built for it, with random priming and short targets.

props.title: ✗ “Quantile = most genes unchanged.”
lines: ✓ It assumes the whole distribution is identical

scenes.title: Move the middle, copy the curve
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Median scaling MOVES THE MIDDLE: it lines up each class by its middle student. Quantile COPIES THE CURVE: it forces every class to have the identical grade curve. DASL READS SCRAPS: short pieces are enough.” Tokens: move the middle = median · copy the curve = quantile · read scraps = DASL. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid. Median scaling moves the middle: it lines up each array by one central value. Quantile copies the curve: every array gets the identical distribution. DASL reads scraps: short pieces of RNA are enough.
Where it breaks: copying the curve is only safe when few genes truly change; very low RNA input still lowers the number of genes detected; and none of these methods measures protein.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Median scaling = most genes unchanged · quantile = whole distribution identical → test before normalizing”, “DASL = random priming + short targets for FFPE · mRNA is not protein”.

cues.text: Median scaling assumes most genes are unchanged while quantile normalization assumes the whole distribution is identical, degraded paraffin-block RNA can be profiled with DASL, and an mRNA change on an array does not by itself prove a protein change.

props.label: Median = most genes unchanged · quantile = whole curve identical
DASL = random priming, short targets · mRNA ≠ protein

explanation.what: Plain language: before comparing arrays you correct for one being brighter than another. Simple scaling lines up the middle; quantile normalization makes every array’s whole spread of values identical. Damaged RNA from paraffin blocks needs an assay that reads short pieces, and an mRNA result is only a transcript result. Scientific terms: global adjustment methods, median correction, trimmed-mean scaling, quantile normalization, class effect, quantro, class-specific quantile normalization, formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) RNA, poly-A tract, DASL (cDNA-mediated annealing, selection, extension and ligation), random priming, post-transcriptional regulation.
explanation.why: Normalization assumptions decide whether a global difference is treated as noise or as biology; a wrong assumption can create false positives, shrink true effects or hide them. Archived FFPE tissue is described as an invaluable resource for cancer research, and protein abundance depends on translation and degradation as well as mRNA level.
explanation.measure: Median or trimmed-mean scaling: one factor per array; assumes most genes are not differentially expressed. Quantile normalization: sort, average each rank, replace, restore order; assumes the whole distribution is the same. DASL: random priming, about 50-nucleotide target; original assay up to 1536 targets; whole-genome version about 24,000 genes; detected 1.5–2-fold changes in FFPE samples. mRNA vs protein (one human cell line): mRNA alone R² ≈ 0.29; with sequence features ≈ 0.67.
explanation.differs: Median scaling (one central value) vs quantile normalization (whole distribution); technical vs biological global differences; whole-data vs class-specific quantile normalization; oligo-dT priming vs random priming; transcript level vs protein level.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: match each normalization method to its assumption, choose an assay for degraded FFPE RNA, or reject the claim that an array mRNA change proves a protein change.

mnemonic.explanation: Separates a one-value shift from a whole-distribution match, and reminds you that DASL works from short RNA pieces.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes the assumption behind quantile normalization of expression arrays?

options.text: The entire intensity distribution is the same across the samples being normalized
options.rationale: Correct. Quantile normalization forces every sample to the same (rank-averaged) distribution, so it assumes the distributions really are the same.

options.text: Only most genes are unchanged; the distribution shape may differ
options.rationale: Incorrect. That weaker assumption fits median or trimmed-mean scaling, which adjusts one central value.

options.text: A set of housekeeping genes is constant across samples
options.rationale: Incorrect. Housekeeping-gene normalization was an early approach that did not work well; quantile normalization uses all values.

options.text: Global differences between samples are biological and must be kept
options.rationale: Incorrect. Global normalization methods assume the opposite: global differences are technical.

questions.stem: A laboratory wants genome-wide expression profiles from archived formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tumour blocks. Which feature of the DASL assay makes it suitable?

options.text: Random priming and a short (about 50-nucleotide) target per probe
options.rationale: Correct. Random priming does not depend on poly-A tails, and short targets suit fragmented RNA.

options.text: Exclusive oligo-dT priming from intact poly-A tails
options.rationale: Incorrect. Many FFPE RNA fragments lack a poly-A tract, which is why DASL does not rely solely on oligo-dT priming.
Incorrect. DASL measures transcripts, not protein.
Incorrect. Normalization is a data-analysis step and does not repair degraded RNA.

questions.stem: A gene shows a 3-fold mRNA increase on an expression array in tumour versus normal tissue. What is the best conclusion?

options.text: The transcript is increased; protein level must be confirmed separately
options.rationale: Correct. Arrays measure mRNA, and translation and protein degradation also determine protein abundance.
Incorrect. mRNA level explains only part of protein-abundance variation.

options.text: The protein must be decreased by feedback
options.rationale: Incorrect. Nothing in the array result predicts a protein decrease; the protein level is simply unmeasured.

options.text: The finding is an artefact because tumour arrays are brighter
options.rationale: Incorrect. A global brightness difference calls for checking the normalization assumption, not for dismissing every finding.

references.citation: Hicks SC, Irizarry RA. quantro: a data-driven approach to guide the choice of an appropriate normalization method. Genome Biol. 2015;16:117. doi:10.1186/s13059-015-0679-0
references.usedFor: Global adjustment methods assume global differences are technical; justified when only a minority of genes are differentially expressed; median correction among data-driven methods; trimmed-mean method assumes most genes are not differentially expressed; quantile normalization assumes the same distribution and its four steps; housekeeping-gene normalization did not work well; quantro tests for global distribution differences; global normalization can remove biological variation.

references.citation: Zhao Y, Wong L, Goh WWB. How to do quantile normalization correctly for gene expression data analyses. Sci Rep. 2020;10(1):15534. doi:10.1038/s41598-020-72664-6
references.usedFor: Quantile normalization assumes similar distributions regardless of class, which holds only when few genes are dysregulated; distortions (false positives, effect-size reduction, masked true effects); cancer as a high class-effect example; class-specific quantile normalization recommended if quantile normalization must be used.

references.citation: Park T, Yi SG, Kang SH, Lee S, Lee YS, Simon R. Evaluation of normalization methods for microarray data. BMC Bioinformatics. 2003;4:33. doi:10.1186/1471-2105-4-33
references.usedFor: Normalization removes systematic (technical) variation; global median normalization of log ratios as a standard method.

references.citation: April C, Klotzle B, Royce T, Wickham-Garcia E, Boyaniwsky T, Izzo J, Cox D, Jones W, Rubio R, Holton K, Matulonis U, Quackenbush J, Fan JB. Whole-genome gene expression profiling of formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissue samples. PLoS One. 2009;4(12):e8162. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0008162
references.usedFor: Formalin modifies adenosines and fragments RNA (up to 50% of fragments may lack poly-A); DASL expansion and principle (random priming, ~50-nt target); original DASL limited to up to 1536 targets; whole-genome DASL covering ~24K RefSeq genes; 1.5–2-fold changes detected in FFPE samples.

references.citation: Vogel C, Abreu Rde S, Ko D, Le SY, Shapiro BA, Burns SC, Sandhu D, Boutz DR, Marcotte EM, Penalva LO. Sequence signatures and mRNA concentration can explain two-thirds of protein abundance variation in a human cell line. Mol Syst Biol. 2010;6:400. doi:10.1038/msb.2010.59
references.usedFor: Post-transcriptional regulation (translation, protein degradation) leads to generally low mRNA–protein correlation; mRNA alone R² = 0.29 in Daoy cells; combined model explains 67% of protein-abundance variation.

claims.text: Global methods assume global differences are technical; median/trimmed-mean scaling assumes most genes are not differentially expressed.
Quantile normalization steps; it assumes the whole distribution is the same across samples.
When many genes change, global normalization can remove biology and distort results; quantro and class-specific quantile normalization as responses.
FFPE RNA damage; DASL random priming, ~50-nt target, up to 1536 targets (original), ~24,000 genes (whole-genome version).
mRNA level explains only part of protein-abundance variation; translation and degradation contribute.
Nylon macroarrays are porous with high autofluorescence, precluding two-colour ratiometric assays (Ch. 70 Hit 9, Trap 1).
